newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African 1996 gold output seen below 500 tonnes.
newsitem.headline: S.African 1996 gold output seen below 500 tonnes.

text.p: South Africa's gold mines will fail to achieve the 500 tonnes of gold production forecast for 1996, mining analysts said on Monday.
But this year will probably mark the low point, with production starting to recover from next year.
The Chamber of Mines on Monday announced output of just 39.6 tonnes of gold in September, compared with 41.2 tonnes August.

Gold production in the first nine months of the year was a meagre 367.8 tonnes, down from 390.6 tonnes a year ago, because of the effects of violence, labour disputes, earth tremors, underground fires and public holidays, analysts said.
The industry is now faced with the near hopeless task of producing on average 44 tonnes of gold for each of this year's remaining three months if it wants to hit 500 tonnes for the year.
"We're not going to make it. It is not going to be as good as we anticipated," said Dave Giese, mining analyst at Smith Borkhum and Co Inc.
Last year production fell 61.5 tonnes to a 40-year-low of 522.4 tonnes. That compares with a record 1,000 tonnes produced in 1970.
Giese said a realistic expectation for the remainder of 1996 was probably a slight improvement to an average 40 tonnes per month, which would mean overall output for 1996 of just under 490 tonnes.
"Without the disruptions that September saw like seismic activity, labour violence, et cetera, we should get a slight lift off in the coming months," he added.

Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd was particularly hard hit by adverse events. In the quarter ended September the group reported a sharp drop in profits and production, dragged down by strikes, violence and fires at its largest mines.
Combined net profit before capital spending was 274.41 million rand compared with 355.86 million rand in the preceding quarter.
But Roger Baxter, senior economist at the Chamber of Mines, said that while output was down, the bigger picture for the industry had to be surveyed.
Certain mines which were forced to close because of violence had performed dismally in September, while other mines had performed fairly satisfactorily, he said.
"You have to look at it in perspective. Violence closed mines for weeks at a time. The rest of the mines didn't do too badly" he said.

Both Baxter and Giese said that 1996 would see the end of the slide in South African output. Looking to the future, they said the groundwork had already been laid for an improvement in 1997 and beyond.
"If all the schemes that the various mining companies have put in place operate efficiently then 1997 will be a base before the bigger mines kick in with additional production," Baxter said.
"Production in the last few months (of this year) will stabilise. A month on month improvement will show from September and could continue into next year," Baxter said.
